paragraphs.text: Good evening, elders and sisters. Good to be able to talk with you again tonight. No new updates on our situation, but I was delighted to be able to go see a bunch of missionaries. I visited missionaries in San Jose del Monte Zone today, not everyone, but most of the missionaries up there, and it was great to see them. They're all doing wonderful.

So let's just jump right into chapter three now of Drawing on the Powers of Heaven. This chapter is entitled The Principles that Govern Faith, and the first section which we'll be discussing tonight has to do with goals—how you achieve goals by drawing on the powers of heaven. The very first part of this is entitled Selecting Righteous Desires, or we could say selecting the right goal.

In order to draw on the powers of heaven, you must systematically decide what you want the Lord to help you accomplish. It's impossible to exercise faith in the powers of heaven at your disposal without having a very specific end in mind. The most serious failing on the part of most members of the Church with respect to faith is their failure to make specific decisions regarding the things they want the Lord to assist them with. For example, unless you systematically make the decision that you want to be instrumental in someone's conversion, the chance that you will play a part in someone's conversion is really quite small.

In Mormon 9:21 we read this: "Behold I say unto you that whoso believeth in Christ, doubting nothing, whatsoever he shall ask the Father in the name of Christ, it shall be granted unto him; and this promise is unto all, even unto the ends of the earth." So in your dealings with the Lord, the need to ask for specific blessings is an absolute requirement. Dedication alone is not enough. You must specifically request blessings, from D&C 11 verse 5: "Therefore, if you will ask of me, ye shall receive; if you will knock, it shall be opened unto you." This same promise is repeated in scriptures at least a hundred times. However, you cannot take advantage of this promise unless you are willing to ask the Lord in faith to help you achieve your desires.

I can promise you, elders and sisters, that the Spirit is a lot more anxious to help you than you are to even be helped, because he knoweth all things. And so the desire on the part of our Father in heaven, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Ghost is intense because of the desire they have to save all of Father's children. And so truly, the Spirit is more willing and more anxious to help us than we probably realize.

If we realized blessings as a direct result of dedication, we would lose sight of the hand of the Lord. Do you understand what I'm saying there? If we just obeyed the law and got the blessing, we would look at this as kind of a mechanical process. And so, yes, we need to obey the law, but we also need to acknowledge the hand of the Lord. We need to acknowledge that the blessing does come from him. And so that's why we can't just focus on dedication. We also still need to ask. When you have the responsibility to actually ask for a specific blessing, that creates a connection between you and God that goes beyond just the keeping of the commandment.

The Lord has said: "...remember that without faith you can do nothing; therefore ask in faith. Trifle not with these things; do not ask for that which you ought not..." This is D&C section 8 verse 10. In D&C 88, 64 and 65, we read this: "Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, it shall be given unto you, that is expedient for you; And if ye ask anything that is not expedient for you, it shall turn unto your condemnation." So this goes to that point of asking for righteous goals as opposed to just asking for things that may or may not be good.

If you remember the occasion where Alma was praying that he could be an angel, so that he could cry with the trump of God to bring salvation to people, and then he realized that even in his desire, it wasn't really appropriate, and so he changed and went a different direction. Reading from the scriptures again: "And now behold, because thou hast done this with such unwearyingness... Behold, I will bless thee forever; and I will make thee mighty in word and in deed, in faith and in works; yea, even that all things shall be done unto thee according to thy word, for thou shalt not ask that which is contrary to my will." That's the key clause. The Lord had already proven that Helaman would only ask for those things that were according to the will of God.

Again this: "...ye must not perform anything unto the Lord save in the first place ye shall pray unto the Father in the name of Christ, that he will consecrate thy performance unto thee, that thy performance may be for the welfare of thy soul." Second Nephi 32:9. Pure motives are a prerequisite to the ability to call down the powers of heaven. The Lord will not sustain your efforts to achieve, excel, or receive special blessings if your desires are vain, if they're selfish, if they're just focused entirely on you.

However, you should realize that you can have an eye single to the glory of God and still desire to excel in athletics, in school, in your vocation. An eye single to the glory of God means that a person's general orientation to life is centered on the gospel of Jesus Christ. This orientation influences a person's conduct and attitude at all times. Generally, how conscientious you are in carrying out your various responsibilities in the Church indicates to what degree your motives are pure. The scripture, Matthew 6:33: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you." If your motives are pure, you'll be entitled to inspiration in determining what desires you should seek. From this, D&C 46:30: "...he that asketh in the Spirit asketh according to the will of God."

The Lord has admonished us to seek his support and inspiration in all our endeavors. You have the assurance that if you have an eye single to the glory of God, you will be inspired to select the righteous desires. It is your responsibility to be certain your desires are righteous. The Lord does not dictate what desires you should strive for. President Spencer W. Kimball made this observation:

"We do believe in setting goals. We live by goals. In athletics, we always have a goal. When we go to school, we have the goal to graduate and get our degrees. Our total existence is goal-oriented. We must have goals to make progress, encouraged by keeping records as the swimmer or the jumper or the runner does. Progress is easier when it's time, checked and measured. Goals are good. Laboring with a distant aim sets the mind at a higher key and puts us at our best. Goals should always be made to a point that they will make us reach and strain. It is most appropriate for you to quietly and with determination set some personal goals in which you will seek to improve by selecting certain things that you will accomplish within a specified period of time. Even if you are headed in the right direction, if you are without momentum, you will have very little influence." All of those quotes are from President Spencer W. Kimball.

Now, here are some guidelines for setting goals. Many of your goals, or we may call it desires, grow out of expectations associated with your job, your schooling, your church calling. Certainly that's the case with us as missionaries. However, it is important that some of your goals or desires are self-imposed. As the Lord says in D&C 58:26 through 29: "For behold, it is not meet that I should command in all things; for he that is compelled in all things, the same is a slothful and not a wise servant; wherefore he receiveth no reward. Verily I say, men should be anxiously engaged in a good cause, and do many things of their own free will, and bring to pass much righteousness; For the power is in them, wherein they are agents unto themselves. And inasmuch as men do good they shall in nowise lose their reward. But he that doeth not anything until he is commanded, and receiveth the commandment with doubtful heart, and keepeth it with slothfulness, the same is damned."

As a general rule, it's much better to focus on a few specific goals at one time rather than trying to focus on many goals at the same time. You should use wisdom in determining how many goals you attempt to focus on at the same time, according to your own personal situation, your ability, and what makes it work for you. Goals, of course, need to be realistic—something you are not currently achieving and something that will require a certain amount of mental exertion. Otherwise, you will not be required to use faith as a principle of power.

You need to realize that the desire may not be easy to achieve, but you must maintain the faith that if you make a determined effort, the Lord will prepare a way for your righteous goals to be accomplished. Your success in achieving the goal will be in direct proportion to your faith and efforts, not your circumstances. Throughout your life, you should follow President Kimball's admonition to set goals for yourself. You should select goals in every facet of your life, not just goals related to your church callings. You are entitled to draw on the powers of heaven in realizing any righteous desire, be it emotional, social, professional, academic, it doesn't matter. Goals are good and God wants you to continue getting better and stronger. Remember that the power of faith has power, dominion, and authority over all things and learn to approach everything you desire to achieve with the power of faith in mind. The Lord is willing and anxious to assist you in achieving your righteous desires.

Now as you set goals for yourself, you should realize that goals fall into two basic categories. One, goals that can be accomplished as a result of the faith that prompts you to action. These are goals where you can see clearly in your mind's eye how you can accomplish these goals through your personal determination and your personal action. For instance, that you will get up at 6 o'clock each morning, that you will refrain from being critical of others, that you will study the scriptures for a certain number of hours per week.

The second type of goal are the goals that require you to draw on the powers of heaven because you cannot see clearly in your mind's eye how those goals can be accomplished. These are goals that cannot be accomplished without the Lord's help—goals that require you to call down the powers of heaven to assist you in fulfilling them. For instance, goals in our missionary service, goals that will allow you to have the kind of profession that you have never seen happen in your family or from any of your friends or any of the people in your circumstance, where you can actually break out of your total environment and rise above anything you've ever seen before. That's going to be something that's going to require God's help because you can't see how you can do it on your own.

Now, it's important to remember that a desire cannot be considered a goal until you're willing to commit yourself and resolve to do everything in your power to achieve the goal. You should not confuse things that you merely consider achieving with those things that you actually determine to achieve. Many of your goals will only involve a personal resolve on your part. In other instances, you will make a commitment to others. And in some cases, you may be willing to promise the Lord that you will do certain things in your effort to qualify yourself to draw on the powers of heaven. You should strive to develop absolute faith in the Lord's promise: "I, the Lord, am bound when ye do what I say."

Finally, this part. Concerning your goals in general, you should remember to consider them as means and not ends. For instance, going on a mission is a goal for many members of the Church. Yet if missionaries are not willing to sacrifice and set specific goals after they are on the mission, then they won't be very successful as a missionary. The same holds true for a temple marriage. Going through the temple is just the beginning of all that goes into a successful marriage. The same is true for goal setting in general. In no instance does the achievement of a goal mean that you have arrived. No matter how many goals you may achieve during a lifetime, you always have to look ahead to new goals. Unless you adopt the point of view that goals are means and not ends, you will experience a letdown every time you achieve a big goal. The achievement of goals should be an ongoing process, not the culmination of an effort that does not lead to a sustained effort to achieve additional goals.

Now, we just want to conclude before we end here with this thought. I think each of you have seen this in your life already, where you'll go through a spurt or a season or a sprint where you'll set a lot of goals. You'll achieve them and then you'll just kind of fall into sort of a plateau, a level of just not doing anything. This is the danger of not having goals already established before you achieve the goal you're working on right now.

I've learned in my life that as I get close to achieving one of my big goals, I have to decide what I'm going for next—what big thing I'm going to be going for next. And then when I achieve that goal I'm working on at the current time, it's a day of celebration, but that's it, because I'm already engaged in and focused on the new goal. In other words, I'm not constantly rising up to a peak and then falling down into a trough of like, 'Oh, I'm not going to do anything right now. I've got nothing to do or I'm bored or I'm this.' I'm constantly driving. And so you're driving towards that goal and as you're getting close to achieving it, you start thinking, what's next? What's next? What's the next big mountain I'm going to climb? What's the next thing I'm going to do? Because I want to get that in my mind, I want to get that goal out there and get it starting to simmer on the pot, so I'm ready to go for it as soon as I get this one done. And boy, then you nail the one you're working on right now, you achieve it, you celebrate for a little while, and then you're right back energized in that pursuit of that new goal. And that's critically important for you.

Okay, so tomorrow—and we will be doing one of these tomorrow—we'll be talking about how you seek for the gifts of the Spirit, how you use the powers of heaven to bring the gifts of the Spirit in so that you can actually use the gifts of the Spirit to achieve your goals. And this is exciting. This is stuff that really can help you. All right, sisters and elders, great to talk with you tonight. I hope this has been useful to you and we'll talk again tomorrow. Love you.
